'''''Abies balsamea''''' or '''balsam fir''' is a North American [[fir]], native to most of eastern and central Canada ([[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]] west to central [[Alberta]]) and the northeastern United States ([[Minnesota]] east to [[Maine]], and south in the [[Appalachian Mountains]] to [[West Virginia]]).<ref>{{PLANTS|symbol=ABBA|taxon=Abies balsamea (balsam fir)|access-date=15 June 2022}}</ref>

== Description ==
Balsam fir is a small to medium-size [[evergreen]] [[tree]] typically {{convert|14|-|20|m}} tall, occasionally reaching a height of {{convert|27|m}}. The narrow conic crown consists of dense, dark-green leaves. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] on young trees is smooth, grey, and with [[resin]] blisters (which tend to spray when ruptured), becoming rough and fissured or scaly on old trees. The [[leaf|leaves]] are flat and needle-like, {{convert|15|to|30|mm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} long, dark green above often with a small patch of [[stomata]] near the tip, and two white stomatal bands below, and a slightly notched tip. They are arranged spirally on the shoot, but with the leaf bases twisted so that the leaves appear to be in two more-or-less horizontal rows on either side of the shoot. The needles become shorter and thicker the higher they are on the tree. The [[seed cones]] are erect, {{convert|40|to|80|mm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} long, dark purple, ripening brown and disintegrating to release the winged [[seed]]s in September.

=== Medicinal ===
For thousands of years Native Americans used balsam fir for medicinal and therapeutic purposes. The needles are eaten directly off the tree by many animals and humans. Higher content dosage is ingested in tea. Balsam fir contains [[vitamin C]], which has been studied for its effects on bacterial and viral infections.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hemilä |first=Harri |date=December 2003 |title=Vitamin C and SARS coronavirus |journal=Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy |volume=52 |issue=6 |pages=1049–1050 |doi=10.1093/jac/dkh002 |pmc=7110025 |pmid=14613951}}</ref>

Balsam fir's essential oil and some of its compounds have shown efficacy against ticks.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Balsam fir (''Abies balsamea'') needles and their essential oil kill overwintering ticks (''Ixodes scapularis'') at cold temperatures|last1=Adamo|first1=Shelley A.|last2=El Nabbout|first2=Amal|last3=Ferguson|first3=Laura V.|last4=Zbarsky|first4=Jeffrey S.|last5=Faraone|first5=Nicoletta|journal=Scientific Reports|volume=12|article-number=12999|year=2022|doi=10.1038/s41598-022-15164-z|doi-access=free|pmc=9338056}}</ref>

=== Reproduction ===
The male reproductive organs generally develop more rapidly and appear sooner than the female organs. The male organs contain microsporangia which divide to form sporogenous tissue, composed of cells which become archesporial cells. These develop into microspores, or pollen-mother cells, once they are rounded and filled with starch grains. When the microspores undergo meiosis in the spring, four haploid [[microspore]]s are produced which eventually become pollen grains. Once the male strobilus has matured the microsporangia are exposed at which point the pollen is released.

The female megasporangiate is larger than the male. It contains bracts and megasporophylls, each of which contains two ovules, arranged in a spiral. These then develop a nucellus in which a mother cell is formed. [[Meiosis]] occurs and a megaspore is produced as the first cell of the megagametophyte. As cell division takes place the nucleus of the megaspore thickens, and cell differentiation occurs to produce prothallial tissue containing an [[Egg cell|ovum]]. The remaining undifferentiated cells then form the endosperm.

When the male structure releases its pollen grains, some fall onto the female [[strobilus]] and reach the ovule. At this point the [[pollen tube]] begins to generate, and eventually the sperm and egg meet at which point [[Fertilisation|fertilization]] occurs.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bakuzis |first1=E.V. |title=Balsam Fir: A Monographic Review |last2=Hansen |first2=Henry L. |last3=Kaufert |first3=Frank H. |date=January 1965 |publisher=University of Minnesota Press |isbn=978-0-8166-6128-2 |location=Minneapolis |pages=2, 8–14}}</ref>

== Varieties ==
There are two varieties:
* ''Abies balsamea'' var. ''balsamea'' (balsam fir) – bracts subtending seed scales short, not visible on the closed cones. Most of the species' range.
* ''Abies balsamea'' var. ''phanerolepis'' (bracted balsam fir or Canaan fir) – bracts subtending seed scales longer, visible on the closed cone. The southeast of the species' range, from southernmost [[Quebec]] to [[West Virginia]]. The name ''Canaan fir'' derives from one of its native localities, the [[Canaan Valley, West Virginia|Canaan Valley]] in West Virginia. Some botanists regard this variety as a natural hybrid between balsam fir and [[Fraser fir]] (''Abies fraseri''), which occurs further south in the Appalachian mountains.  This produces a slight change in color, making it appear similar to a true Fraser Fir.

== Ecology ==
[[File:Carter Dome seen from Mt Hight.JPG|thumb|left|upright|Balsam fir [[krummholz]] on [[Mount Hight]], [[New Hampshire]]]]

Balsam firs are very shade tolerant, and tend to grow in cool climates, ideally with a mean annual temperature of {{convert|40|F}}, with consistent moisture at their roots.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Walters |first1=Michael B. |last2=Reich |first2=Peter B. |date=July 2000 |title=Seed Size, Nitrogen Supply, and Growth Rate Affect Tree Seedling Survival in Deep Shade |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1890/0012-9658(2000)081[1887:SSNSAG]2.0.CO;2 |journal=Ecology |language=en |volume=81 |issue=7 |pages=1887–1901 |doi=10.1890/0012-9658(2000)081[1887:SSNSAG]2.0.CO;2 |issn=0012-9658 |hdl-access=free |hdl=11299/175095}}</ref> Low moisture and high temperature have been identified as important factors restricting its range.<ref>{{cite journal |date=2024-10-18 |first1=Narayani |last1=Barve |first2=Uzma |last2=Ashraf |first3=Vijay |last3=Barve |first4=Marlon E. |last4=Cobos |first5=Claudia |last5=Nuñez-Penichet |first6=Andrew |last6=Townsend Peterson |title=Revisiting plant hardiness zones to include multiple climatic stress dimensions |article-number=110824 |doi=10.1016/j.isci.2024.110824 |journal=iScience |eissn=2589-0042 |volume=27 |issue=10|pmid=39435139 |pmc=11491728 |bibcode=2024iSci...27k0824B }}</ref> They typically grow in the following four forest types:
* [[Swamp]] – swamp forest types never completely dry out, so balsam firs have constant access to water. The ground is covered in [[sphagnum]] and other mosses. In swamps, balsam firs grow densely and slowly, and are slender.
* Flat – sometimes referred to as "dry swamps", these areas are better drained than swamps but still retain moisture well. [[Fern moss]] covers the ground and there is a possibility of ground rot. In flat areas balsam fir grows fast, tall, and large, mixed with [[Picea rubens|red spruce]].
* Hardwood slope – ground rot is common in this well-drained area, and [[Plant litter|leaf litter]] covers the [[forest floor]]. Balsam firs grow fast, tall, and large along with big [[hardwood]] trees such as [[Betula alleghaniensis|yellow birch]], [[Acer saccharum|sugar maple]] and [[beech]].
* Mountain top – On mountain tops, stands of balsam fir occasionally develop [[fir wave]]s. They often grow at an elevation of {{convert|2500 to 5000|ft|order=flip|abbr=on}} in pure strands, or in association with [[black spruce]], [[white spruce]], [[white birch]], and trembling [[aspen]]. The development is similar to that in swamps with slow growth resulting in slender, short trees. Some of the low branches touch the ground, and may grow roots to produce an independent tree.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zon |first=Raphael |date=March 25, 1914 |title=Balsam Fir |url=https://archive.org/stream/balsamfir55zonr#page/n1/mode/2up |journal=Bulletin of the U.S. Department of Agriculture |volume=55 |pages=2–7}}</ref>

The foliage is browsed by moose and deer.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Eastern Region |publisher=Knopf |year=1980 |isbn=0-394-50760-6 |location=New York |page=278}}</ref> The seeds are eaten by [[American red squirrel]]s, grouse, and pine mice;<ref>{{Cite book |last=Peattie |first=Donald Culross |author-link=Donald C. Peattie |title=A Natural History of Western Trees |publisher=[[Bonanza Books]] |year=1953 |location=New York |page=188}}</ref> the tree also provides food for [[crossbill]]s and [[chickadee]]s, as well as shelter for moose, [[snowshoe hare]]s, [[white-tailed deer]], [[ruffed grouse]], and other small mammals and songbirds. The needles are eaten by some [[lepidoptera]]n caterpillars, for example the [[Io moth]] (''Automeris io'').

''Abies balsamea'' is one of the most cold-hardy trees known, surviving at temperatures as low as {{convert|-45 |C|F|abbr=on}} ([[USDA Hardiness Zone]] 2). Specimens even showed no ill effects when immersed in [[liquid nitrogen]] at {{convert|-196 |C|F|abbr=on}}.<ref name="GYMN">{{Cite web |title=Abies balsamea |url=https://www.conifers.org/pi/Abies_balsamea.php |access-date=8 August 2019 |publisher=The Gymnosperm Database}}</ref>

It is short-lived by conifer standards, the oldest specimen being 245 years old as of 1996. The tallest and widest specimen had a height of {{convert|31.7|m|ft}} and a [[Diameter at breast height|DBH]] of {{convert|406|cm|in}}.<ref>{{cite web |date=2009 |author=BeeEnvironment |title=Balsam Fir at 560 Mt. Hope Road in Fairfield, Pennsylvania, United States |url=https://www.monumentaltrees.com/en/usa/pennsylvania/adams/27657_560mthoperoad |website=Monumental Trees }}{{Dead link|date=November 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=1997–2025 |first=Christopher J. |last=Earle |title=Abies balsamea |url=https://www.conifers.org/pi/Abies_balsamea.php |website=The Gymnosperm Database}}</ref>

===Conservation status===
It is listed as endangered in [[Connecticut]]. This status applies to native populations only.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20151023162806/http://www.ct.gov/deep/lib/deep/wildlife/pdf_files/nongame/ETS15.pdf "Connecticut's Endangered, Threatened and Special Concern Species 2015"]. State of Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection Bureau of Natural Resources. Retrieved 17 January 2018. (Note: This list is newer than the one used by plants.usda.gov and is more up-to-date.)</ref>

=== Pests ===
The balsam fir is the preferred main host of the [[Choristoneura fumiferana|eastern spruce budworm]], which is a major destructive pest throughout the eastern United States and Canada.<ref name="Powell">{{Cite book |title=Biosystematic Studies of Conifer-Feeding Choristoneura (Lepidoptera Tortricidae) in the Western United States |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-09796-4 |editor-last=Powell |editor-first=Jerry A.}}{{page needed|date=August 2024}}</ref> During cyclical population outbreaks, major defoliation of the balsam fir can occur, which may significantly reduce [[Growth rings|radial growth]].<ref name="blais32">{{Cite journal |last=Blais |first=J. R. |year=1958 |title=The Vulnerability of Balsam Fir to Spruce Budworm Attack in Northwestern Ontario, with Special Reference to the Physiological Age of the Tree |journal=The Forestry Chronicle |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=405–422 |doi=10.5558/tfc34405-4 |doi-access=free}}</ref> This can kill the tree. An outbreak in Quebec in 1957 killed over 75% of balsam fir in some stands.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Blais |first1=J. R. |last2=Martineau |first2=R. |year=1960 |title=A Recent Spruce Budworm Outbreak in the Lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe Peninsula with Reference to Aerial Spraying Operations |journal=The Forestry Chronicle |volume=36 |issue=3 |pages=209–224 |doi=10.5558/tfc36209-3 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

The needles of balsam fir can be infected by the fungus ''[[Delphinella balsameae]]''.<ref name="Guertin et al 2018">{{Cite journal |last1=Guertin |first1=Julien F. |last2=Zitouni |first2=Mina |last3=Tanguay |first3=Philippe |last4=Hogue |first4=Richard |last5=Beaulieu |first5=Carole |date=2018 |title=Detection of ''Delphinella'' shoot blight in plantations of balsam fir (''Abies balsamea'') Christmas trees in Quebec, Canada |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Pathology |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=87–97 |doi=10.1080/07060661.2018.1547791 |s2cid=92569747}}</ref>

Balsam fir is also the most susceptible tree in Eastern Canada to red heart rot, caused by the fungus [[Stereum sanguinolentum]]. This fungus causes the heartwood to decay and turn a red-brown colour, potentially killing the tree if the disease spreads sufficiently. This can be partially mitigated by avoiding bark damage when logging and mitigating sun scald by not thinning excessively.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Callan |first1=B.E. |title=Red heart rot |url=https://tidcf.nrcan.gc.ca/en/diseases-caused-by-pathogens/factsheet/418 |website=Natural Resources Canada |publisher=Canadian Forest Service |access-date=14 December 2025}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
===Christmas trees===
Both varieties of the species are very popular as [[Christmas trees]], particularly in the northeastern United States. Balsam firs cut for Christmas are typically grown on large plantations, not taken from the forest. The balsam fir is one of the greatest exports of Quebec and [[New England]]. It is celebrated for its rich green needles, natural conical shape, and needle retention after being cut, and it is notably the most fragrant of all Christmas tree varieties.<ref>{{Cite book |title=A Guide to Useful Woods of the World |publisher=Forest Products Society |year=2001 |isbn=1-892529-15-7 |editor-last=Flynn |editor-first=James H. |edition=2nd |location=Madison, WI |pages=2–3 |language=en |editor-last2=Holder |editor-first2=Charles D.}}</ref>

The balsam fir was used six times for the US [[Capitol Christmas Tree]] between 1964 and 2019.<ref name = GYMN/>

===Horticulture===
''Abies balsamea'' is also grown as an ornamental tree for parks and gardens. Very [[hardiness (plants)|hardy]] down to {{convert| -20|C|F|abbr=on}} or below, it requires a sheltered spot in full sun. The dwarf [[cultivar]] ''A. balsamea'' 'Hudson' (Hudson fir), grows to only {{convert|1 |m|ft|abbr=on}} tall by {{convert|1.5 |m|ft|abbr=on}} broad, and has distinctive blue-green foliage with pale undersides. It does not bear cones. It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=RHS Plant Selector Abies balsamea Hudsonia Group 'Hudson' AGM / RHS Gardening |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/222400/i-Abies-balsamea-i-(Hudsonia-Group)-Hudsonia/Details |access-date=August 21, 2016 |publisher=Apps.rhs.org.uk}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=July 2017 |title=AGM Plants - Ornamental |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf |access-date=7 August 2019 |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |page=1}}</ref>

== Other uses ==
[[File:BalsamFirEssOil.png|thumb|upright|Balsam fir essential oil in clear glass vial]]
The resin is used to produce [[Canada balsam]], and was traditionally used as a [[Common cold|cold]] remedy and as a [[glue]] for glasses, optical instrument components, and for preparing permanent mounts of microscope specimens. Given its use as a traditional remedy and the relatively high ascorbic acid content of its needles, historian Jacques Mathieu has argued that the balsam fir was the "[[aneda]]" that cured [[scurvy]] during the second expedition into Canada of [[Jacques Cartier]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mathieu |first=Jacques |title=L'Annedda: L'arbre de vie |publisher=Septentrion |year=2009 |location=Quebec |lang=fr|isbn=978-2-89448-591-0}}{{page needed|date=August 2024}}</ref> The [[wood]] is milled for [[Framing (construction)|framing lumber]] (part of [[Spruce-pine-fir|SPF]] lumber), siding and pulped for [[paper]] manufacture. Balsam fir oil is an EPA approved nontoxic rodent repellent. The balsam fir is also used as an [[air freshener]] and as [[incense]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-08-20 |title=Balsam fir oil (129035) Fact Sheet |url=http://www.epa.gov/opp00001/biopesticides/ingredients/factsheets/factsheet_129035.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081211090413/http://www.epa.gov/opp00001/biopesticides/ingredients/factsheets/factsheet_129035.htm |archive-date=December 11, 2008 |access-date=August 21, 2016 |website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]}}</ref>

===Native American ethnobotany===
[[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]] use it for a variety of medicinal purposes.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Abies balsamea |url=http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Abies+balsamea |access-date=August 21, 2016 |website=North American Ethnobotany DB}}</ref>

The [[Abenaki]] use the gum for slight itches and as an antiseptic ointment.{{sfn|Rousseau|1947|p=164}} They stuff the leaves,{{sfn|Rousseau|1947|p=155}} needles, and wood into pillows as a [[panacea]].{{sfn|Rousseau|1947|pp=163-164}}

The [[Algonquin people]] of [[Quebec]] apply a poultice of the gum to open sores, insect bites, boils and infections, use the needles as a [[sudatory]] for women after childbirth and for other purposes, use the roots for heart disease, use the needles to make a laxative tea, and use the needles for making [[poultice]]s.<ref>{{Cite report |title=Algonquin Ethnobotany: An Interpretation of Aboriginal Adaptation in South Western Quebec |last=Black |first=Meredith Jean |publisher=National Museums of Canada |location=Ottawa |volume=65 |page=124 |year=1980 |series=Mercury Series}}</ref>

The [[Atikamekw]] chew the sap as a cold remedy, and use the boughs as mats for the tent floor.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Raymond |first=Marcel |year=1945 |title=Notes Ethnobotaniques Sur Les Tete-De-Boule De Manouan |journal=Contributions de l'Institut Botanique de l'Université de Montréal |volume=55 |page=118}}</ref>

The [[Cree]] use the pitch for menstrual irregularity, and take an infusion of the bark and sometimes the wood for coughs. They use the pitch and grease as an ointment for [[scabies]] and [[Boil (infection)|boil]]s. They apply a [[poultice]] of pitch applied to cuts. They also use a decoction of pitch and [[Fish oil|sturgeon oil]] used for [[tuberculosis]], and take an infusion of bark for tuberculosis. They also use the boughs to make brush shelters and use the wood to make paddles.<ref>{{Cite report |title=Wild Plant Use by the Woods Cree (Nihithawak) of East-Central Saskatchewan |last=Leighton |first=Anna L. |publisher=National Museums of Canada |location=Ottawa |page=21 |year=1985 |series=Mercury Series}}</ref>

The [[Innu people]] grate the inner bark and eat it to benefit their diet.{{sfn|Speck|1917|p=313}}

The [[Iroquois]] use a steam from a decoction of branches as a bath for [[rheumatism]] and [[parturition]], and ingest a decoction of the plant for rheumatism. They take a compound decoction for colds and coughs, sometimes mixing it with alcohol. They apply a compound decoction of the plant for cuts, sprains, bruises and sores.{{sfn|Herrick|1977|p=269}} They apply a [[poultice]] of the gum and dried beaver kidneys for cancer.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rousseau |first=Jacques |year=1945 |title=Le Folklore Botanique De Caughnawaga |journal=Contributions de l'Institut Botanique de l'Université de Montréal |volume=55 |page=37}}</ref> They also take a compound decoction in the early stages of tuberculosis, and they use the plant for bedwetting and [[gonorrhea]].{{sfn|Herrick|1977|p=270}}

The [[Maliseet]] use the juice of the plant as a laxative,{{sfn|Mechling|1959|p=244}} use the pitch in medicines,<ref name="Speck, Frank G 1952, page 6">{{Cite journal |last1=Speck |first1=Frank G. |last2=Dexter |first2=R.W. |year=1952 |title=Utilization of Animals and Plants by the Malecite Indians of New Brunswick |journal=Journal of the Washington Academy of Sciences |volume=42 |page=6}}</ref> and use an infusion of the bark, sometimes mixed with spruce and [[tamarack]] bark, for [[gonorrhea]].{{sfn|Mechling|1959|p=257}} They use the needles and branches as pillows and bedding, the roots as thread, and use the pitch to waterproof seams in canoes.<ref name="Speck, Frank G 1952, page 6" />

The [[Menominee]] use the inner bark as a seasoner for medicines, take an infusion of the inner bark for chest pain, and use the liquid balsam pressed from the trunk for colds and pulmonary troubles. They also use the inner bark as a poultice for unspecified illnesses.<ref name="Smith, Huron H. 1923, page 45">{{Cite journal |last=Smith |first=Huron H. |year=1923 |title=Ethnobotany of the Menomini Indians |journal=Bulletin of the Public Museum of the City of Milwaukee |volume=4 |page=45}}</ref> They also apply gum from plant blisters to sores.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Densmore |first=Francis |year=1932 |title=Menominee Music |journal=SI-BAE Bulletin |volume=102 |page=132}}</ref>

The [[Miꞌkmaq]] use a poultice of inner bark for an unspecified purpose,<ref name="Smith, Huron H. 1923, page 45" /> use the buds, cones and inner bark for diarrhea, use the gum for burns, colds, fractures, sores and wounds, use the cones for colic, and use the buds as a laxative. They also use the bark used for gonorrhea and buds used as a laxative.<ref>Chandler, R. Frank, Lois Freeman and Shirley N. Hooper, 1979, Herbal Remedies of the Maritime Indians, Journal of Ethnopharmacology 1:49-68, page 53</ref> They use the boughs to make beds, use the bark to make a beverage, and use the wood for kindling and fuel.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Speck |first1=Frank G. |last2=Dexter |first2=R.W. |year=1951 |title=Utilization of Animals and Plants by the Micmac Indians of New Brunswick |journal=Journal of the Washington Academy of Sciences |volume=41 |page=258}}</ref>

The [[Ojibwe]] melt the gum on warm stones and inhale the fumes for headache.{{sfn|Densmore|1928|p=338}} They also use a [[decoction]] of the root as an herbal steam for rheumatic joints.{{sfn|Densmore|1928|p=338}} They also combine the gum with [[Bear's grease#Native American use|bear's grease]] and use it as an ointment for hair.{{sfn|Densmore|1928|p=350}} They use the needle-like leaves in as part of ceremony involving the [[sweat bath]], and use the gum for colds and inhale the leaf smoke for colds.{{sfn|Smith|1932|p=378}} They use the plant as a cough medicine.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reagan |first=Albert B. |year=1928 |title=Plants Used by the Bois Fort Chippewa (Ojibwa) Indians of Minnesota |journal=Wisconsin Archeologist |volume=7 |issue=4 |page=244}}</ref> The gum is used for sores and a compound containing leaves is used as wash. The liquid balsam from bark blisters is used for sore eyes.{{sfn|Smith|1932|p=378}} They boil the resin twice and add it to [[suet]] or fat to make a canoe pitch.{{sfn|Smith|1932|p=420}} The bark gum is taken for chest soreness from colds, applied to cuts and sores, and decoction of the bark is used to induce sweating. The bark gum is also taken for [[gonorrhea]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hoffman |first=W.J. |year=1891 |title=The Midewiwin or 'Grand Medicine Society' of the Ojibwa |journal=SI-BAE Annual Report |volume=7 |page=198}}</ref>

The [[Penobscot]] smear the sap over sores, burns, and cuts.{{sfn|Speck|1917|p=309}}

The [[Potawatomi]] use the needles to make pillows, believing that the aroma prevented one from getting a cold.<ref name="Smith, Huron H. 1933, page 121">{{Cite journal |last=Smith |first=Huron H. |year=1933 |title=Ethnobotany of the Forest Potawatomi Indians |journal=Bulletin of the Public Museum of the City of Milwaukee |volume=7 |page=121}}</ref> They also use the balsam gum as a salve for sores, and take an infusion of the bark for tuberculosis and other internal afflictions.<ref name="Smith, Huron H. 1933, page 121" />

== Tree emblem ==
Balsam fir is the [[Provincial tree emblems of Canada|provincial tree]] of [[New Brunswick]].
